lessons.title: Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions
lessons.summary: In a right triangle, sine is opposite/hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite/adjacent relative to a chosen acute angle.
objectives: Explain opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions.
Calculate and interpret sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, cotangent using sin²θ+cos²θ=1.
Recognize why this claim fails: The opposite side stays the same when the reference angle changes.

sections.heading: Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions
paragraphs: Relative to θ in a right triangle, opposite changes if you choose the other acute angle, while the hypotenuse stays opposite the right angle. SOH-CAH-TOA gives sine, cosine and tangent; reciprocals give cosecant, secant and cotangent where denominators are nonzero. At 30°, (sin,cos)=(1/2,√3/2); at 45°, both are 1/√2; at 60°, they swap. Squaring opposite²+adjacent²=hypotenuse² proves sin²θ+cos²θ=1.
In a right triangle, sine is opposite/hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite/adjacent relative to a chosen acute angle.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Similar right triangles explain why the ratios depend on the angle rather than the overall size. Pythagoras divided by hypotenuse² gives sin²θ+cos²θ=1. Reciprocal ratios require nonzero denominators. At endpoint angles some ratios are undefined, so the tool reports that rather than a huge misleading number.

Choose the reference angle before naming opposite and adjacent sides. Select the ratio that uses the known and requested sides. Keep degree units explicit. For exact special angles use the 30–60–90 or 45–45–90 triangle values, distinguishing those from rounded decimals.

lessons.summary: A tangent touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that contact point. An external point has two tangent segments of equal length.
objectives: Explain tangent, secant and point of contact.

sections.heading: Tangent, secant and point of contact
paragraphs: A tangent meets the circle at one point; a secant crosses it at two. The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. An exterior point has two equal tangent segments: their right triangles share the centre-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii, so RHS proves equality. A point on the circle has one tangent line, even though the tangent-segment length measured from that point is zero.
A tangent touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that contact point. An external point has two tangent segments of equal length.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The radius and tangent segment form a right triangle with the centre-to-external-point distance as hypotenuse. An inside point has no real tangent; a point on the circle has one tangent line. Counting tangent lines is different from treating the zero-length on-circle segment as an external construction.

Compare OP with radius r first. For an external point compute √(OP²−r²). Use the equal-tangent theorem for other lengths, and use the radius perpendicularity only at the actual contact point. Verify the radicand is nonnegative.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer

sections.heading: Number of tangents from interior/on/exterior points
paragraphs: A tangent meets the circle at one point; a secant crosses it at two. The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. An exterior point has two equal tangent segments: their right triangles share the centre-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii, so RHS proves equality. A point on the circle has one tangent line, even though the tangent-segment length measured from that point is zero.
A tangent touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that contact point. An external point has two tangent segments of equal length.

sections.heading: Number of tangents from interior/on/exterior points
paragraphs: A tangent meets the circle at one point; a secant crosses it at two. The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. An exterior point has two equal tangent segments: their right triangles share the centre-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii, so RHS proves equality. A point on the circle has one tangent line, even though the tangent-segment length measured from that point is zero.
